name: Treaty at Camp Keyes (1851), unratified California treaty B
aka: Treaty B of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 3 set apart, to be 'forever held for the sole use and occupancy' of the signing tribes, two tracts: one between the Cahwai river and King's river, bounded by the lands of the Camp Barbour treaty; the other from Tulare lake near the mouth of King's river to the big bend of the San Joaquin, bounded by the lands of the Camp Belt treaty.

Brood mares and a stallion, cows and a bull, ploughs, harness, work mules or horses, oxen, axes, hoes, spades, picks or mattocks and seed (Kappler, vol. 4, p. 1094, as excerpted by Oklahoma State University).
A farmer to instruct the tribes, a superior and assistant school teachers, and a school-house (Kappler, vol. 4, as excerpted by Oklahoma State University).

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty B in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

source.title: Robert F. Heizer, The Eighteen Unratified Treaties of 1851-1852 between the California Indians and the United States Government (1972)
source.publisher: Archaeological Research Facility, University of California, Berkeley

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

source.title: Act of May 18, 1928, ch. 624, 45 Stat. 602 (Indians of California jurisdictional act)

breaches.quote: the loss to the said Indians on account of their failure to secure the lands and compensation provided for in the eighteen unratified treaties

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 277, 278, 279 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

plain.promised: Two tracts near Kings River and Tulare lake held forever for the signing tribes, plus livestock, ploughs, tools, seed, a farmer and school teachers with a school-house.
plain.happened: The Senate refused to ratify the treaty on July 8, 1852, and kept it secret until 1905. The tribes' lands were taken without the reserved tract or compensation.
plain.today: The treaty remains unratified. A 1928 Act let California Indians sue for the promised lands and compensation; the amount finally paid has not been traced.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: Picayune Rancheria of Chukchansi Indians of California; Santa Rosa Indian Community of the Santa Rosa Rancheria; Santa Rosa Indian Community of the Santa Rosa Rancheria, California; Table Mountain Rancheria of California; Tule River Indian Tribe of the Tule River Reservation; Tule River Indian Tribe of the Tule River Reservation, California; Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians of the Tuolumne Rancheria of California.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.
Heizer notes the 1852 message lists treaty B under May 13, 1851, while the schedule gives May 30, 1851.

Heizer (1972) prints only Article 3 of this treaty and Oklahoma State University gives excerpts, so any beef and flour article, the other mechanics and the duration of the provisions were not checked.

The Senate's rejection date is given as July 8, 1852 by Heizer (1972, introduction), but the Senate clerk's 1904 search quoted in the National Archives' Prologue article (2013) gives July 2, 1852; the Senate Executive Journal was not opened to settle it.

Audit 2026-11-08: promises rewritten from treaty B's own text (Heizer 1972, and Kappler vol. 4 as excerpted by Oklahoma State University); the four generic promises copied across the California files ('Article 3 or 4', beef and flour 'during 1851 and 1852', staff 'for at least five years') did not fit this treaty or could not be checked for it.
